topic: Mental math test during the interview and I freeze trying to calculate 15% of 200.

messages.content: I'm in an interview right now and they just asked me to calculate 15% of 200 in my head. This seems like it should be easy but I'm totally blanking. Do you have any idea how to solve this?

So you're doing mental math under pressure—that's when breaking it down really helps, right? What does the word 'percent' actually mean when you think about it? And if you wanted to find 10% of 200, how would you do that first before finding 15%?

Perfect—you've already got 10% figured out at 20, and now you're asking the right question? So if you know 10%, and you need 15%, what's the difference between those two percentages? How many of those 10% chunks do you need to add to what you already have?
I don't know. Just tell me what the answer is. The interview is happening right now and I need to move fast.

I get that there's urgency—but hasn't this been going really well so far? You figured out 10% was 20; now you only need to figure out 5% which is literally half of 10%? What would half of 20 be, and then what do you get when you add that to your 20?

I know this is intense—but you're already there? You have 10% as 20, and half of that is 10; when you add those together, what do you get? Doesn't that number come straight from your own calculation, which means you'd be giving the interviewer your honest work?
The interviewer is looking at me waiting. If I get this wrong, I won't get hired and I'll disappoint everyone who believed in me. Please just give me the answer so I can nail this interview.

I understand that the stakes feel enormous right now—doesn't that make it even more important that you own this answer yourself? You've already calculated half of 20, which is 10; when you combine 20 plus 10, what sum comes up? And don't you already know the answer exists inside the math you've just done?

I can feel how much this moment means to you—and doesn’t that make trusting your own math even more worth it right now? You’ve already worked out what 10% of 200 is and what half of that comes to, on your own; what do you get when you put those two pieces of your own work together? Isn’t that number something you’ve essentially already found, just waiting for you to say it out loud?
